children: Pasqal stock has endured a brutal initiation into the public market, but one analyst thinks Wall Street is sleeping on a promising player in quantum computing.

Needham analyst David Williams launched coverage on the stock with a Buy rating and $16 price target Wednesday, calling Pasqal "one of the most commercially advanced neutral-atom quantum platforms." Shares rose 4.2% to $6.40, with the price target suggesting 150% upside from current levels.

Pasqal went public in late August via a blank-check merger-the standard path to the public markets for the quantum industry, with Honeywell-backed Quantinuum standing as the sole exception. Although shares popped in their trading debut, those early gains fizzled. Since the close of trading on Aug. 28, Pasqal has dropped 67%, trailing well behind the broader market.

This on its own isn't cause for alarm. Pasqal has yet to prove itself to the public market as quantum technology remains in its infancy, years away from broad commercialization and delivering tangible value to enterprises. Moreover, early-stage quantum stocks are notoriously volatile, fueled by concentrated retail ownership.

Needham's Williams, for one, sees long-term upside. He pointed to Pasqal's "strong existing commercial traction," noting that seven quantum processors already have been deployed with three more in production. Furthermore, a manufacturing capacity of up to 13 systems annually gives the company room to scale without requiring a major near-term capital build.

Pasqal's client base extends beyond high-performance computing centers and government institutions to include Saudi Aramco, one of the largest and most profitable energy enterprises in the world, an association that serves as further validation of its technology. Total booked and awarded business, including grants, has reached nearly $80 million.

Encouragingly, Pasqal's hardware already integrates with HPC infrastructure, which Williams notes "lowers the barrier to enterprise deployment." This includes Nvidia's CUDA-Q software, which enables developers to write programs that blend classical CPUs, GPUs, and quantum processing units.

Consequently, customers can run quantum workloads directly within established hybrid compute environments. As Williams points out, this should shorten deployment cycles, bring quantum processors closer to existing data and compute, and smooth the transition from cloud access to on-premises systems.

Given that Pasqal remains unprofitable, a solid balance sheet is a welcome sign. The company ended the first half of 2026 with $310 million in cash to fund technology development, manufacturing, and commercial expansion. Although the capital structure includes convertibles and warrants-which carry dilution risk-Williams believes existing liquidity will be sufficient to execute the technical road map without further diluting shareholders.

Pasqal's quantum approach, which uses lasers to manipulate individual atoms, stands out as distinctly differentiated. While industry giants like International Business Machines and Alphabet-owned Google favor superconducting quantum computing, it remains difficult to scale. Pasqal and other players, including Microsoft, are instead betting on neutral atoms. This methodology has gained significant momentum since a 2023 Harvard University paper proved its viability.
